Hidden structure of Jack Littlewood-Richardson Coefficients
Ryan Mickler

Abstract
. We argue that Jack Littlewood-Richardson coefficients g μ ​ ν λ ​ ( α ) g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}(\alpha) are specialisations of certain novel polynomials. For the triple of partitions ( μ , ν , λ ) = ( 21 , 21 , 321 ) (\mu,\nu,\lambda)=(21,21,321) , we prove the corresponding polynomial is invariant under S 6 × ℤ 2 S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} , which is identified as the automorphism group of the Johnson graph J ⁡ ( 6 , 3 ) J(6,3) . We conjecture that these polynomials exhibit a factorization property on certain hyperplanes, which is a consequence of compatibility relations between polynomials associated to adjacent triples in the Young graph. As a consequence of this, we conjecture that the difference of adjacent Jack Littlewood-Richardson coefficients is divisible by the shared hook length.



1.
Background

In this work, we continue the project begun in
[
7
]
of investigating the structure of Jack Littlewood-Richardson coefficients
g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
, particularly for the case of
\mu=\{2,1\}
,
\nu=\{2,1\}
,
\lambda=\{3,2,1\}
which is given by

g_{21,21}^{321}=\frac{6\alpha(2+11\alpha+2\alpha^{2})}{(1+2\alpha)(2+\alpha)(2+3\alpha)(3+2\alpha)}.

That the numerator of this coefficient is a
non-negative
polynomial in
\alpha
is the content of the so-called Stanley conjecture of
[
9
]
. It this this conjecture that has motivated the present investigation.

This work culminates in a conjecture that reveals hidden structure in these coefficients.

Conjecture 1.1

(see (
6.4
))
.

For two triples of partitions
(\mu_{1},\nu_{1},\lambda_{1})
,
(\mu_{2},\nu_{2},\lambda_{2})
that differ by a single box move (a ‘pivot’) in one of the pairs in the triples, say at
b_{1}\in\sigma_{1}
,
b_{2}\in\sigma_{2}
, so that

h_{\sigma_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}({b_{1}})=h_{\sigma_{2}}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}({b_{2}}),

then we have

(1)

g_{\mu_{1}\nu_{1};\lambda_{1}}(\alpha)\equiv\,g_{\mu_{2}\nu_{2};\lambda_{2}}(\alpha)\mod h_{\sigma_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}({b_{1}}).

For example, we look at the coefficients for two triples that differ by a single box move (for the box
b=(0,0)
in
\{321\}
)

(2)

\displaystyle g_{21,21;321}(\alpha)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 6\alpha^{4}(1+2\alpha)(2+\alpha)(2+11\alpha+2\alpha^{2}),

(3)

\displaystyle g_{21,21;2211}(\alpha)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 4\alpha^{4}(1+2\alpha)^{2}(3+\alpha)(4+\alpha).

We see that the
difference
of these polynomials

g_{21,21;321}(\alpha)-g_{21,21;2211}(\alpha)=2\alpha^{4}(1+2\alpha){\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(3+2\alpha)}(-4+6\alpha+\alpha^{2})

is divisible by
h_{2211}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}(b)=h_{321}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}(b)={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(3+2\alpha)}
.

We use the notation from

]
which we briefly summarize here. Let

represent

{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}

For a box

, or

\alpha
-hook lengths

h^{*}_{\lambda}(b)=h_{\lambda}^{\prime}(b)=h_{\lambda}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(b)

.
.

(4)

\mathrm{ev}:{\bm{h}}_{\sigma}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}(b)\mapsto[{\bm{h}}_{\sigma}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}(b)]:=h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}_{\sigma}(b)\in\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]

Inside a tableau, we denote upper hook symbol by

{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}

and lower hook symbol by

{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}

.
Note that the hook choices for the boxes in
\lambda
are in the denominator.
Equivalently, a Stanley diagram is a rational function of the hook symbols,

{\bm{D}}\leftrightarrow\frac{\left(\prod_{b\in\mu}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{D}}_{b}}\right)\left(\prod_{b\in\nu}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{D}}_{b}}\right)}{\left(\prod_{b\in\lambda}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{D}}_{b}}\right)}.

For a diagram
{\bm{D}}
, we let
{\bm{D}}^{\prime}
be the polynomial in the hook symbols given by
{\bm{D}}^{\prime}:={\bf{j}}_{\lambda}\,{\bm{D}}
, where
{\bf{j}}_{\lambda}=\prod_{b\in\lambda}({\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}})
. That is,

{\bm{D}}^{\prime}=\left(\prod_{b\in\mu}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{D}}_{b}}\right)\left(\prod_{b\in\nu}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{D}}_{b}}\right)\left(\prod_{b\in\lambda}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\overline{{\bm{D}}}_{b}}\right).

The motivating conjecture for this investigation is due to Richard Stanley, for whom we’ve named the constructions above.

Conjecture 1.3

(“Strong” Stanley Conjecture
[
9
, C8.5]
)
.

If
c_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}=1
, then there exists a Stanley diagram
\bm{D}\in\mathsf{SD}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
such that the corresponding Jack LR coefficient is computed by evaluation

g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}=[\bm{D}].

Furthermore,
{\bm{D}}
may be taken to have an equal number of upper (and hence, lower) hooks in the numerator and denominator of the diagram.

The following generalization of Stanley’s conjecture (
1.3
) to all cases
c_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}>1
was given in
[
7
]
.

Definition 1.4
.

A
Stanley Sum

{\bm{s}}\in\mathsf{SS}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
is an element in the
\mathbb{Z}
-span of Stanley Diagrams

{\bm{s}}=\sum_{\bm{D}\,\in\mathsf{SD}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}}c_{\bm{D}}\,\bm{D}\in\mathsf{SS}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda},

with
c_{\bm{D}}\in\mathbb{Z}
. The evaluation map extends linearly to such sums.

Conjecture 1.5

(General Structure,
[
7
]
)
.

For each triple of partitions
\mu,\nu,\lambda
, there exists a Stanley sum,

(5)

{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}=\sum_{\bm{D}\in\mathsf{SD}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}}c_{\bm{D}}\,\bm{D},\qquad c_{\bm{D}}\in\mathbb{Z},

such that the corresponding Jack LR coefficient is computed by evaluation,

(6)

g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}=[{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}].

We call such a Stanley sum
{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
a
Rule
for
g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
.

As was discussed in
[
7
]
,
the form (
5
) is not overly restrictive as there are
2^{|\lambda|+|\mu|+|\nu|}
free integer coefficients
c_{\bm{D}}
, leaving many degrees of freedom.

We define
{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu;\lambda}:=\left({\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}\right)^{\prime}
as a polynomial form of the rule (
[{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu;\lambda}]
is sometimes referred to as a Stanley Coefficient).

1.2.
Observations

We begin this paper by observing the following properties of the Stanley sum (
1.1.1
).

Observation 1.8
.

For each diagram
{\bm{D}}
in the support (i.e.
c_{\bm{D}}\neq 0
) of
{\bm{g}_{\star}}
, we have

(198)

{\bm{D}}_{b_{3}}={\bm{D}}_{c_{1}}=\overline{{\bm{D}}}_{c_{6}}.

Thus, we consider a new virtual box,
\tilde{b}_{3}
, that refers to the value of all three.
We black out the boxes at
c_{1}
and
c_{6}
, as they are determined by the hook assignment at
b_{3}
. From now on we only refer to the remaining ten boxes.

For a subset of boxes
J
, let
{\bm{D}}^{J}
be the diagram
{\bm{D}}
however with the hooks flipped at all boxes in
J
.

Observation 1.9
.

The Stanley sum (
1.1.1
) has the following decomposition,

(219)

{\bm{g}_{\star}}=7{\bm{X}}-2\sum_{b}{\bm{X}}^{\{b\}}+\sum_{\{a,b\}\in\Theta}{\bm{X}}^{\{a,b\}},

where
\Theta
is a set of fifteen pairs of boxes.
The pairs
\Theta
constitute the edges of the Petersen graph
{\mathrm{P}}
, with vertices labelled as

(220)

c_{4}
c_{2}
\tilde{b}_{3}
a_{1}
c_{5}
c_{3}
a_{3}
b_{2}
a_{2}
b_{1}

This identification defines an action of
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})=S_{5}
on boxes.

This surprising structure underlines many of the constructions in this work. The Petersen graph
{\mathrm{P}}
is most usefully described at the Kneser graph
K(5,2)
, in which vertices are 2-subsets
I=(ij)
of a set with five elements,
[5]
, and
I\sim J
if
I
and
J
are disjoint. The
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})=S_{5}
action is then the permutation action on
[5]
acting on 2-subsets.

2.
The Hook Space

2.1.
Windows

We begin by recalling the definitions of windows from the previous work
[
7
]
.

Definition 2.1
.

For a fixed triple of partitions
T=(\mu,\nu;\lambda)
, a
window

W
is a triple of partitions
(\mu_{W},\nu_{W};\lambda_{W})
such that
W
reduces to the
root
triple
T
under a sequence of three moves,

•

King-Tollu-Toumazet
[
6
]
factorization on the triple,

•

Windowing on the pair
\mu\subset\lambda
,

•

Windowing on the pair
\nu\subset\lambda
.

Thus a window
W
comes with an inclusion of boxes from
b\in T\mapsto b_{W}\in W
. A
window family

{\mathcal{W}}=\{W_{i}\}_{i\in V}
is a parametrised collection of windows.

Example 2.2
.

For the root
T=\{1,1,1^{2}\}
, consider the window family
{\mathcal{W}}=\{W_{m,n}\}
with

W_{m,n}=\{1^{m+1},(n+1),(n+1)1^{m+1}\},

\{a,b,c,d\}
of

are included as

Conjecture 2.3

(Jack Windowing,
[
7
]
)
.

Let
W
be a window for a triple
T
. There exists a rule
{\bm{g}}_{T}
, such that a rule
{\bm{g}}_{W}
can be constructed with the following properties.

•

The boxes outside of
T\subset W
are assigned a specific choice of hooks
\bm{F}_{W}

•

The boxes inside
T\subset W
are assigned the same rule
{\bm{g}}_{T}
(extended by linearity).

Symbolically,

(232)

{\bm{g}}_{W}=\bm{F}_{W}\circ({\bm{g}}_{T})_{W}.

Example 2.4
.

Returning to the window in example (
2.2

2.2.
Hook spaces

To proceed, we introduce
hook spaces
. These are essentially the space of Stanley sums modulo the kernel of the evaluation map for a given window family.

Here, we have the hook lengths

\displaystyle h_{\lambda}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(d)=m+1+(n+1)\alpha,

\displaystyle h_{\mu}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(a)=m+1+(0)\alpha,

\displaystyle h_{\nu}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(b)=0+(n+1)\alpha,\,\qquad

\displaystyle h_{\lambda}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(c)=\alpha.\qquad\qquad\quad

We note the single relation holds for all
m,n

h_{\lambda}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(d)-h_{\mu}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(a)-h_{\nu}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(b)=0

Thus the linear sum

(273)

{\bf{r}}_{1}:={\bm{h}}_{\lambda}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(d)-{\bm{h}}_{\mu}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(a)-{\bm{h}}_{\nu}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(b),

is in the kernel of the evaluation map.

The relation (
273
) captures the configuration of the family
W_{m,n}
as imposed on the hook symbols of the root of the family. We introduce a formal variable
{\bf{\beta}}
, which evaluates to
[{\bf{\beta}}]=\alpha-1
.

Definition 2.7
.

For a root triple
\{\mu,\nu,\lambda\}
with a window family
{\mathcal{W}}
, define the
hook space

\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}})
as the intersection of the kernels of the evaluation map
ev_{W}
for each window
W\in{\mathcal{W}}
acting on homogeneous polynomials in the hook variables and
\beta
.

\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}})=\bigcap_{W\in{\mathcal{W}}}\mathrm{Ker}\left(\mathrm{ev}_{W}:{\mathrm{Sym}}({\bm{h}},{\bf{\beta}})\to{\mathbb{Q}}[\alpha]\right).

By design, the evaluation map
\mathsf{SS}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}\to\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]
factors through the hook space. Let
\iota^{*}:\mathsf{SS}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}\to\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}})
be the pullback to the hook space.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{SS}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbb{Q}}[\alpha]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ev}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\mathrm{ev}}}

Since
h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\mu}(b)-h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mu}(b)=\alpha-1
for any box
b
, we always have the basic linear relations

(276)

{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\sigma}(b)-{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\sigma}(b)-{\bf{\beta}}\in\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}}).

Note that if
{\mathcal{W}}^{\prime}\subset{\mathcal{W}}
is a smaller family of windows, then

\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}})\twoheadrightarrow\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}}^{\prime})\twoheadrightarrow\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}({\mathcal{W}}_{0})

where
{\mathcal{W}}_{0}:=\{\mu\nu,\lambda\}
is the family consisting of only the trivial window of the root triple. This is generated by the many relations between the usual hook lengths.

In general, there are many relations in the hook space. For example, for any two boxes
a<b
such that
a\wedge b\in\sigma
, we have

{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\sigma}(a\vee b)-{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\sigma}(a)-{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\sigma}(b)+{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\sigma}(a\wedge b)=0.

For the rest of this paper, we will be focusing on the following object.

Definition 2.9
.

The
Jack Littlewood-Richardson Polynomial

{{\bm{G}}}
for a rule
{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
that solves a window family
{\mathcal{W}}
is the pullback of
{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu;\lambda}:=\bf{j}_{\lambda}\cdot{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
to the hook space.

{{\bm{G}}}:=\iota^{*}{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu;\lambda}\in\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}({\mathcal{W}}).

The objective of this paper is to demonstrate that the polynomial
{{\bm{G}}}
has properties that are not manifest in the Stanley sum
{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu;\lambda}
.

The hook lengths for the triple
\{21,21,321\}
in the families (
2.10
) are given by (with
r_{2}n_{4}=0
):

\displaystyle h_{a_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{1}+(n_{1}+1)\alpha

\displaystyle h_{a_{2}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{1}+m_{2}+r_{1}+1+(n_{1}+n_{2}+2)\alpha

\displaystyle h_{a_{3}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{2}+(n_{2}+1)\alpha

\displaystyle h_{b_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{3}+\alpha

\displaystyle h_{b_{2}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{3}+r_{1}+r_{2}+1+(n_{4}+2)\alpha

(327)

\displaystyle h_{b_{3}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle(n_{4}+1)\alpha

\displaystyle h_{c_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle\alpha

\displaystyle h_{c_{2}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{1}+m_{3}+r_{1}+1+(n_{1}+2)\alpha

\displaystyle h_{c_{3}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle r_{1}+\alpha

\displaystyle h_{c_{4}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}+r_{1}+r_{2}+2+(n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{4}+3)\alpha

\displaystyle h_{c_{5}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle m_{2}+r_{1}+r_{2}+1+(n_{2}+n_{4}+2)\alpha

\displaystyle h_{c_{6}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:

\displaystyle r_{2}+\alpha.

For the virtual hook
\tilde{b}_{3}
motivated by (
198
), we define

h_{\tilde{b}_{3}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}:=\alpha^{-1}h_{b_{3}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}h_{c_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}h_{c_{6}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}\equiv r_{2}+(n_{4}+1)\alpha\mod r_{2}n_{4}.

In particular, for our special rule
{\bm{g}_{\star}}
(
1.1.1
) for this family (
2.10
), we define
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}:=\iota^{*}{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
. We analyse the structure of this particular hook space by finding an abundance of four-term relations between the various hooks.

Example 2.11
.

Consider the vertex
a_{2}
, adjacent to
\{a_{1},a_{3},c_{3}\}
, we find

-h^{U}_{a_{2}}+h^{U}_{a_{1}}+h^{U}_{a_{3}}+h^{U}_{c_{3}}-\beta=0.

We write
a\sim b
for two boxes that are adjacent in the Petersen graph (
220
).
Let
x_{b}:=(-1)^{{\bm{X}}_{b}/{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}
, where
{\bm{X}}
is given by (
1.2
). Thus

{\bm{X}}=\prod_{b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{X}}_{b}}=\prod_{b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{x_{b}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}

Proposition 2.12
.

For each
b
and each window in the family
W\in{\mathcal{W}}
(
2.10
), the relation
[{\bm{f}}_{b}]_{W}=0
holds, where

(328)

{\bm{f}}_{b}:=-x_{b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{X}}_{b}}+\sum_{a:a\sim b}x_{a}{\bm{h}}_{a}^{{\bm{X}}_{a}}-\beta.

The ten relations
{\bm{f}}_{b}
span
\mathsf{R}_{21,21;321}({\mathcal{W}})
, which is
5
-dimensional.

Proof.

We verify this by direct calculation, referencing the table (
2.10
).

To show the spanning property, we use the claw relations to express the five hooks
\{a_{2},b_{2},c_{2},c_{4},c_{5}\}
in terms of the five independent hooks
\{a_{1},a_{3},b_{1},\tilde{b}_{3},c_{3}\}
and
\beta
. These five are clearly linearly independent. The relations at
{\bm{f}}_{a_{2}}
and
{\bm{f}}_{b_{2}}
immediately give

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{1}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{3}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{3}}-\beta,

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{b_{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{b_{1}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{3}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\tilde{b}_{3}}-\beta.

Similarly, the remaining three are resolved from the relations:

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{5}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{3}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{3}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\tilde{b}_{3}}-\beta,

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{4}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{1}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{3}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{b_{1}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{3}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\tilde{b}_{3}}-2\beta,

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{1}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{b_{1}}+h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{3}}-\beta.

Thus all ten hooks are determined by
\{h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{1}},h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{a_{3}},h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{b_{1}},h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\tilde{b}_{3}},h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{c_{3}}\}
and
\beta
, so
\mathsf{R}_{21,21;321}({\mathcal{W}})
is at most
5
-dimensional. Since the five independent hooks are unconstrained, the dimension is exactly
5
.
∎

The above result is a more concrete manifestation of the Petersen graph, as it captures the relations between the hooks.

2.4.
Summary

The primary object of our attention is the particular Jack
Littlewood-Richardson polynomial that lives in the Hook Space,

(329)

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}:=\iota^{*}{\bm{g}_{\star}}\in\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321}({\mathcal{W}}).

3.
Symmetries

We will also consider maps between hook rings. We start with automorphisms.

Definition 3.1
.

A
hook automorphism

\psi\in{\mathrm{hkAut}}(\mathsf{R})

of a hook space
\mathsf{R}
is a signed map between hook variables
\psi:{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}\mapsto\pm{\bm{h}}_{b^{\prime}}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{B}}}}
that preserves all kernel relations. Given the relations (
276
), for each
b\in\sigma,{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}\in\{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}},{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}\}
such a map must be of the form

\rho:{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}_{\sigma}(b)\mapsto{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}_{\sigma^{\prime}}(b^{\prime})

or

\rho:{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}_{\sigma}(b)\mapsto-{\bm{h}}^{\bar{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}_{\sigma^{\prime}}(b^{\prime}).

Lemma 3.2
.

The action of
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})=S_{5}
on boxes from Observation
1.9
lifts to hook automorphisms given by

(330)

g:{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}\mapsto x_{g.b/b}{\bm{h}}_{g.b}^{x_{g.b/b}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}},

That is,

{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})\subset{\mathrm{hkAut}}(\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321}({\mathcal{W}})).

Proof.

We directly check that this
S_{5}
action on
{\bm{h}}_{b}
permutes the relations (
328
), i.e.
g.{\bm{f}}_{b}={\bm{f}}_{g.b}
, and thus descends to an action on the hook space.
∎

Lemma 3.3
.

The Stanley sum
{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
is invariant under this
S_{5}
action, and thus so is the Jack LR polynomial
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}:=\iota^{*}{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
.

Proof.

We look at each of the terms in the expression (
219
). Firstly, we show that
{\bm{X}}
is invariant under this action.

g.{\bm{X}}=g.\prod_{b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{x_{b}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}=\prod_{b}x_{g.b/b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{x_{g.b}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}=\left(\prod_{b}x_{g.b/b}\right){\bm{X}}

As each generator of
S_{5}
flips hooks in pairs, we get
g.{\bm{X}}=(-1)^{2k}{\bm{X}}
. Similarly,
g.{\bm{X}}^{\{b\}}={\bm{X}}^{\{g.b\}}
.
∎

Thus we can write the expression (
219
) as sum of three orbits of this
S_{5}
action

(379)

{\bm{g}_{\star}}=7\mathscr{O}_{\emptyset}-2\mathscr{O}_{\bullet}+1\mathscr{O}_{\hbox to7.59pt{\vbox to3.39pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.69702pt\lower-1.69702pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 2.35 0 C 2.35 1.3 1.3 2.35 0 2.35 C -1.3 2.35 -2.35 1.3 -2.35 0 C -2.35 -1.3 -1.3 -2.35 0 -2.35 C 1.3 -2.35 2.35 -1.3 2.35 0 Z M 0 0}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

where the subscript indicates the subgraph structure of
{\mathrm{P}}
that has flipped hooks (relative to
{\bm{X}}
). Thus this Petersen structure is manifest in the Stanley sum
{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
(
219
). However, we will find that the Stanley
polynomial

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}:=\iota^{*}{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
has a
non-manifest enlargement
of this Automorphism group to
S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, which is the Automorphism group of the Johnson graph
J(6,3)
. To demonstrate this, we need a change of basis in the hook space.

3.1.
\ell
basis

We consider the change of variables that is more suited to the Petersen symmetry.

Definition 3.4
.

For a fixed Stanley diagram
{\bm{D}}
, we define the
\ell
basis relative to
{\bm{D}}
as

(380)

\ell_{b}:=(-1)^{{\bm{D}}_{b}/{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}({\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}+{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}})=(-1)^{{\bm{D}}_{b}/{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}(2{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}-(-1)^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}/{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}\beta).

If not mentioned, then we take the reference diagram
{\bm{D}}
to be all upper hooks,
{\bm{D}}_{b}={\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}},\forall b
.

When considering the main triple
\{21,21,321\}
, we work relative to the diagram
{\bm{X}}
, defined in (
1.2
). We can express the hook variables as

(381)

x_{b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\ell_{b}+x_{b}(-1)^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}/{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}\beta).

Corollary 3.5
.

With the change of coordinates (
381
), the action of
S_{5}
on the
\ell
variables is the
permutation representation

{V_{\mathrm{P}}}:=\oplus_{b\in{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathbb{C}}\{\ell_{b}\}
of the Petersen graph,

g.\ell_{b}=\ell_{g.b}.

The four-term hook relations (
328
) are expressed as the
claw
relations

(382)

{\bm{f}}_{b}:=\ell_{b}-\sum_{a\sim b}\ell_{a}=(1\text{-}A)\ell_{b},

where
A
is the adjacency matrix of the Petersen graph
{\mathrm{P}}
,

A.\ell_{b}:=\sum_{a:a\sim b}\ell_{a}.

Thus, a function
F
on
{\mathrm{P}}
is in the linear span of the claw relations (
382
) if
F=(1\text{-}A)G
, for another function
G
.

Any graph automorphism group preserves edges and so naturally commutes with the adjacency matrix. The spectrum of
A
is well known (c.f.
[
4
, §9.1]
), and the action of
S_{5}
on the
\ell
basis commutes with the action of the adjacency matrix
A
, and decomposes as
\mathrm{Im}(1\text{-}A)\oplus\ker(1\text{-}A)

(383)

{V_{\mathrm{P}}}=\left(V^{(3)}_{\{5\}}\oplus V^{(-2)}_{\{4,1\}}\right)\oplus V^{(1)}_{\{3,2\}}

Where
V^{k}_{\lambda}
carries
A
-eigenvalue
k
and
S_{5}
-representation corresponding to the partition
\lambda
.
Here
V^{(3)}_{\{5\}}
is the one-dimensional representation generated by

(384)

\sum_{b}{\bm{f}}_{b}=-2\sum_{b}\ell_{b}.

Corollary 3.6
.

The hook space of the triple
\{21,21,321\}
is

(385)

\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321}\cong{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V^{(1)}_{\{3,2\}}[{\bf{\beta}}]).

This simple algebraic description justifies the definition of the hook space. We remind the reader of the distinction between two polynomials,

{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V_{{\mathrm{P}}}[{\bf{\beta}}])^{S_{5}},\qquad{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V^{(1)}_{\{3,2\}}[{\bf{\beta}}])^{S_{5}}

We will demonstrate that
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}
has additional symmetries that are not shared with
{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
.

3.2.
Conjugation Symmetry

We’ve noted that the hook space
\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321}
has a
S_{5}={\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})
symmetry. In addition to this, we observe all the relations (
382
) are linear homogeneous in the
\ell
variables.

Corollary 3.7
.

The hook space has the additional
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
conjugation symmetry

(386)

C:\ell_{b}\to-\ell_{b}.

Thus, the hook automorphism group contains
S_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}\subseteq{\mathrm{hkAut}}(\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321})
.

That is, flipping all boxes is a symmetry of the relations (
328
).
We will spend considerable effort proving the following theorem.

Theorem 3.8
.

The Jack LR polynomial
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\in\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321}
is invariant under this additional
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
.

It is manifestly clear that
{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
does not have this symmetry, as
7{\bm{X}}\in{\bm{g}_{\star}}
, however the coefficient of
\bar{\bm{X}}
is zero.

We prove Theorem (
3.8
) via an equivalent statement (
3.22
) in a later section. First, we need to expand the Stanley sum
{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}
in the
\ell
basis.

3.3.
Orbit sums

In this section we produce an expression of the form

(387)

{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}=\sum_{I}\beta^{|I|}w_{I}\ell_{{\mathrm{H}}/I},

in terms of the monomials
\ell_{J}=\prod_{j\in J}\ell_{j}
, for
J
a subset of the vertices of
{\mathrm{H}}
.In order to do this, we introduce some intermediate constructions.

3.3.1.
K
-values

It was noted in
[
7
]
that for a rule
{\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}=\sum_{\bm{D}}c_{\bm{D}}\,{\bm{D}}
, the sum of all the coefficients
c_{\bm{D}}
, henceforth denoted
K_{\emptyset}
, recovers the Schur Littlewood-Richardson coefficient. That is

(388)

\displaystyle K_{\emptyset}({\bm{g}}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda})

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\sum_{{\bm{D}}}c_{{\bm{D}}}

(389)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}.

In the case of our Stanley sum (
219
) we have

K_{\emptyset}({\bm{g}_{\star}})=7(1)-2(10)+(15)=2=c_{21,21}^{321}.

We situate
K_{\emptyset}
as the first term in a sequence of integers, computed via a linear transform.

Definition 3.9
.

Fix a choice of a reference Stanley diagram
{\bm{B}}
. For each subset
I
of the set of boxes
{\mathrm{H}}
, define the
K
-values
of a Stanley sum
{\bm{s}}=\sum_{\bm{D}}c_{\bm{D}}\,{\bm{D}}
as

(390)

K_{I}^{\bm{B}}({\bm{s}}):=\sum_{{\bm{D}}\,:\,{\bm{D}}_{I}={\bm{B}}_{I}}c_{\bm{D}}.

That is, sum all the coefficients
c_{\bm{D}}
for those
{\bm{D}}
that agree with the reference
{\bm{B}}
on the subset
I
.
In this way, we map the integer coefficients
\{c_{\bm{D}}\}
to the set of integer coefficients
\{K^{\bm{B}}_{I}\}
indexed by the subsets of the set of boxes.

We need to fix some notation before progressing. We use
\bar{\bm{B}}
to denote the diagram with all flipped hooks of
{\bm{B}}
. Let
{\bm{B}}^{J}
be the diagram with boxes
b\in J
flipped relative to
{\bm{B}}
:

(391)

{\bm{B}}^{J}:=\prod_{b\notin J}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}\prod_{b\in J}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\bar{\bm{B}}_{b}}.

Note
\bar{\bm{B}}={\bm{B}}^{\mathrm{H}}
.
Let
{\bm{B}}\wedge{\bm{D}}=\{i\in{\mathrm{H}}:{\bm{D}}_{i}={\bm{B}}_{i}\}
be the set of boxes where
{\bm{D}}
agrees with
{\bm{B}}
. I.e.
{\bm{B}}\wedge\bar{\bm{B}}^{J}=J
.
Let
{\bm{B}}_{I}
be just the subset hook choices associated to the subset of boxes
I\subseteq{\mathrm{H}}
.
We introduce the sign notation

(392)

(-1)^{{\bm{A}}_{I}/{\bm{B}}_{I}}:=(-1)^{|\{i\in I:{\bm{A}}_{i}\neq{\bm{B}}_{i}\}|}

Recall the following basic result.

Lemma 3.10

(Möbius Inversion - c.f
[
10
, §3.8.3]
)
.

Let
H
be a finite set, and let
f,g:\mathcal{P}(H)\to\mathbb{R}
be functions on the power set of
H
. If
g
is the sum of
f
over supersets:

g(I)=\sum_{J\supseteq I}f(J),

then
f
can be recovered from
g
via the alternating sum:

f(I)=\sum_{J\supseteq I}(-1)^{|J\setminus I|}g(J).

We use this to show

Proposition 3.11
.

For each Stanley diagram
{\bm{B}}
, the values

K^{\bm{B}}:\{c_{\bm{D}}:{\bm{D}}\in\mathcal{H}\}\to\{K^{\bm{B}}_{I}:I\subseteq{\mathrm{H}}\}

is invertible.
The Inverse map is given by

(393)

c_{{\bm{D}}}=\sum_{J\supseteq{\bm{B}}\wedge{\bm{D}}}(-1)^{|J|-|{\bm{B}}\wedge{\bm{D}}|}K_{J}^{{\bm{B}}}

Proof.

We have

K_{I}^{\bm{B}}=\sum_{{\bm{D}}:{\bm{B}}\wedge{\bm{D}}\supseteq I}c_{\bm{D}}=\sum_{J:J\supseteq I}c_{\bar{\bm{B}}^{J}},

Applying Lemma (
3.10
) with
g(I)=K_{I}^{\bm{B}}
and
f(J)=c_{\bar{\bm{B}}^{J}}
yields the result. I.e.

c_{\bar{\bm{B}}^{I}}=\sum_{J\supseteq I}(-1)^{|J\setminus I|}K^{B}_{J}.

∎

The dependence of
K_{I}
on
{\bm{B}}
is expressed in the following Lemma.

Lemma 3.12
.

Let
{\bm{A}}^{b}
be equal to
{\bm{A}}
but with a single hook at
b
flipped, then

(394)

K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}^{b}}=\begin{cases}-K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}}+K_{I\setminus b}^{{\bm{A}}},\quad\text{ for }b\in I\\
K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}},\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\text{ for }b\notin I\\
\end{cases}

Thus, the values
\{K_{J}^{{\bm{A}}}\}
can be determined from
\{K_{I}^{{\bm{B}}}\}
by the formula

(395)

K_{J}^{{\bm{A}}}=\sum_{I\subseteq J\,:\,J\setminus I\subseteq{\bm{A}}/{\bm{B}}}(-1)^{{\bm{A}}_{I}/{\bm{B}}_{I}}K_{I}^{{\bm{B}}},

where

{\bm{A}}/{\bm{B}}:=\{i:{\bm{A}}_{i}\neq{\bm{B}}_{i}\}.

Proof.

Then by using the definition (
390
), for
I
with
b\in I
, we have

K_{I\setminus b}^{{\bm{A}}}=K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}}+K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}^{b}}

So

K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}^{b}}=-K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}}+K_{I\setminus b}^{{\bm{A}}}

However, for
I
with
b\notin I
, we have

K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}^{b}}=K_{I}^{{\bm{A}}}

The result follows from multiple single flips.
∎

Corollary 3.13
.

A Stanley sum
{\bm{s}}
can be expressed in terms of its
K
-values as

(396)

\displaystyle{\bm{s}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{{\bm{D}}}\left(\sum_{I\supseteq{\bm{B}}\wedge{\bm{D}}}(-1)^{|I|-|{\bm{B}}\wedge{\bm{D}}|}K_{I}^{{\bm{B}}}({\bm{s}})\right){\bm{D}}

(397)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{J\subseteq{\mathrm{H}}}\left(\sum_{I\supseteq J}(-1)^{|I\setminus J|}K_{I}^{{\bm{B}}}({\bm{s}})\right)\bar{\bm{B}}^{J}.

3.3.2.
Kernel functions

Theorem 3.14

(Kernel functions)
.

Fix a Stanley diagram
{\bm{B}}
and a linear polynomial in hook variables and
\beta
,

{\bm{f}}:=\sum_{b\in Y}a_{b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}+d\,\beta,\qquad Y\subseteq{\mathrm{H}}.

Set
\sigma_{b}:=(-1)^{{\bm{B}}_{b}/{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}
(
+1
for
{\bm{B}}_{b}={\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}
,
-1
for
{\bm{B}}_{b}={\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}
), encoding the
\beta
-shift
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\bar{\bm{B}}_{b}}={\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}+\sigma_{b}\beta
, and define the
kernel function
as the
Y
-supported Stanley sum

(398)

{\bm{k}}_{\bm{f}}^{\bm{B}}\;:=\;\sum_{L\subseteq Y}c_{L}\,{\bm{B}}^{L},\qquad c_{L}:=(-1)^{|L|}\Bigl(d-\sum_{b\in Y\setminus L}\sigma_{b}a_{b}\Bigr).

Then, the following relation holds as polynomials in the variables
{\bm{h}},\beta
:

(399)

{\bm{k}}_{\bm{f}}^{\bm{B}}=(-1)^{|Y|}\,\sigma_{Y}\,{\bm{h}}_{\bar{Y}}^{\bm{B}}\cdot\beta^{|Y|-1}\cdot{\bm{f}},

where
\sigma_{Y}=\prod_{b\in Y}\sigma_{b}
and
{\bm{h}}_{\bar{Y}}^{\bm{B}}=\prod_{b\in\bar{Y}}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}
.

In particular, if
[{\bm{f}}]=0
in the evaluation ring, then
[{\bm{k}}_{\bm{f}}^{\bm{B}}]=0
as well.

Its
K
-values follow from the definition: since
K^{\bm{B}}_{I}({\bm{B}}^{L})=[I\cap L=\emptyset]
, only
L\subseteq Y\setminus I
contribute, and the resulting alternating sum vanishes for
|Y\setminus I|\geq 2
. Concretely,

(400)

K^{\bm{B}}_{I}({\bm{k}}_{\bm{f}}^{\bm{B}})=\begin{cases}d-\sum_{b\in Y}\sigma_{b}a_{b}&I\supseteq Y,\\
-\sigma_{b}a_{b}&I\cap Y=Y\setminus\{b\}\ (b\in Y),\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Proof of Theorem
3.14
.

Write
{\bm{k}}:={\bm{k}}_{\bm{f}}^{\bm{B}}
.

Using
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\bar{\bm{B}}_{b}}={\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}+\sigma_{b}\beta
, each diagram
{\bm{B}}^{L}
(
L\subseteq Y
) factors as

{\bm{B}}^{L}={\bm{h}}_{\bar{Y}}^{\bm{B}}\cdot\prod_{b\in Y\setminus L}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}\cdot\prod_{b\in L}({\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}+\sigma_{b}\beta).

Expanding the
L
-product:

\prod_{b\in L}({\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}+\sigma_{b}\beta)=\sum_{T\subseteq L}\beta^{|T|}\sigma_{T}\prod_{b\in L\setminus T}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}},

so

\frac{{\bm{k}}}{{\bm{h}}_{\bar{Y}}^{\bm{B}}}=\sum_{L\subseteq Y}c_{L}\sum_{T\subseteq L}\beta^{|T|}\sigma_{T}\prod_{b\in Y\setminus T}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}=\sum_{T\subseteq Y}\beta^{|T|}\sigma_{T}\,\tilde{c}^{(T)}\prod_{b\in Y\setminus T}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}},

where we swapped the order of summation and collected the sum
\tilde{c}^{(T)}=\sum_{L\supseteq T}c_{L}
.

By Lemma
3.10
on the power set of
Y
, the sum
\tilde{c}^{(T)}
is uniquely characterised by the inverse relation

c_{L}=\sum_{T\supseteq L}(-1)^{|T\setminus L|}\,\tilde{c}^{(T)}.

We claim:

(401)

\tilde{c}^{(T)}=\begin{cases}0&|T|\leq|Y|-2,\\
(-1)^{|Y|}\,\sigma_{b}a_{b}&T=Y\setminus\{b\},\\
(-1)^{|Y|}\,d&T=Y.\end{cases}

By the uniqueness of Möbius inversion, it suffices to verify that (
401
) satisfies the inverse relation, i.e. reproduces
c_{L}
. For
L\subseteq Y
, only
T=Y
and
T=Y\setminus\{b\}
for
b\notin L
contribute:

\displaystyle\sum_{T\supseteq L}(-1)^{|T\setminus L|}\tilde{c}^{(T)}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{|Y\setminus L|}(-1)^{|Y|}d+\sum_{b\notin L}(-1)^{|Y\setminus L|-1}(-1)^{|Y|}\sigma_{b}a_{b}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{|L|}\Bigl(d-\!\!\sum_{b\in Y\setminus L}\!\sigma_{b}a_{b}\Bigr)=c_{L}.

Hence only
|T|\in\{|Y|-1,|Y|\}
contribute to
{\bm{k}}/{\bm{h}}_{\bar{Y}}^{\bm{B}}
, giving

\beta^{|Y|-1}\!\sum_{b\in Y}\sigma_{Y\setminus\{b\}}(-1)^{|Y|}\sigma_{b}a_{b}\,{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}+\beta^{|Y|}\sigma_{Y}(-1)^{|Y|}d=(-1)^{|Y|}\sigma_{Y}\beta^{|Y|-1}\Bigl(\sum_{b\in Y}a_{b}{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{B}}_{b}}+d\,\beta\Bigr),

using
\sigma_{Y\setminus\{b\}}\sigma_{b}=\sigma_{Y}
. The bracket is
{\bm{f}}
, proving (
399
).
∎

Lemma 3.15
.

For the claw relations (
328
) with
Y={\mathrm{cl}}(b)=\{b\}\cup\{a:a\sim b\}
and any
{\bm{B}}
with
{\bm{B}}_{Y}={\bm{X}}_{Y}
, the kernel sum
{\bm{k}}^{\bm{B}}_{{\bm{f}}_{b}}
is given by the ten-term Stanley sum

(402)

{\bm{k}}^{\bm{B}}_{{\bm{f}}_{b}}\;:=\;k_{f}^{0}-(k_{f}^{0})^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)},\qquad k_{f}^{0}\;:=\;-2\bar{\bm{B}}^{\{b\}}+\sum_{a\sim b}\bar{\bm{B}}^{\{b,a\}}-\bar{\bm{B}}^{Y}.

Proof.

Apply Theorem
3.14
with
Y={\mathrm{cl}}(b)
. Under the natural frame
{\bm{B}}_{Y}={\bm{X}}_{Y}
, the claw relation (
328
) gives
\sigma_{b}a_{b}=+1
and
\sigma_{a}a_{a}=-1
for
a\sim b
, with
d=-1
. Evaluating the coefficients (
398
) on each
L\subseteq Y
, write
\epsilon:=[b\in L]
and
k:=|\{a\sim b:a\notin L\}|
:

\sum_{b^{\prime}\in Y\setminus L}\!\sigma_{b^{\prime}}a_{b^{\prime}}=(1-\epsilon)-k,\qquad c_{L}=(-1)^{|L|}(\epsilon+k-2).

Hence
c_{L}=0
exactly when
\epsilon+k=2
: the three leaf-singletons
L=\{a\}
(
\epsilon=0,k=2
) and the three triples
L=Y\setminus\{a\}
(
\epsilon=1,k=1
),
a\sim b
. The remaining ten
L\subseteq Y
carry the coefficients

c_{\emptyset}=+1,\quad c_{\{b\}}=-2,\quad c_{\{b,a\}}=+1,\quad c_{\{a,a^{\prime}\}}=-1,\quad c_{Y\setminus\{b\}}=+2,\quad c_{Y}=-1,

which assemble as
k_{f}^{0}-(k_{f}^{0})^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}
in (
402
).
∎

3.3.3.
Summary

We summarize the results of the above as follows. For
{\mathrm{P}}
the Petersen graph, let
\ell_{b}
be a variable for each of the 10 vertices
b\in P
,
{V_{\mathrm{P}}}=\mathbb{Z}[P]
is the dimension 10 permutation module of
Aut(P)=S_{5}
. Consider the following
S_{5}
-invariant polynomial, in the variables
\ell_{b},\beta
, expressed as the sum over all subsets
I
of the vertices of
{\mathrm{P}}
.

2^{|{\mathrm{P}}|}{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}:=\sum_{I\subseteq{\mathrm{P}}}w_{P/I}\ell_{I}\beta^{|{\mathrm{P}}/I|}\,\,\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V_{\mathrm{P}}[{\bf{\beta}}])^{S_{5}},

where
\ell_{I}=\prod_{b\in I}\ell_{b}
, and the
S_{5}
-invariant weight
c_{J}\in\mathbb{Z}
for a subset
J
is given by

(407)

w_{J}:=2(2e_{J}-|J|+1),

where
e_{J}
is the number of edges in the subgraph of
{\mathrm{P}}
on the vertices
J
. We have that

2^{|{\mathrm{P}}|}{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}=2(\prod_{b\in{\mathrm{P}}}\ell_{b})\beta^{0}+\ldots+42\beta^{10}.

Note that
f
has coefficients of both signs, e.g. for the subset
I\subset{\mathrm{P}}
of four isolated vertices, then
c_{I}=-6
.

3.4.
Orbit Sums

Since the weights
w_{I}
are invariant under
S_{5}
, we group the terms of (
) according to the
S_{5}
orbits of subsets of vertices. Let
\mathscr{O}_{k}
be the set of
S_{5}
-orbits of
k
-subsets of vertices of
{\mathrm{P}}
. For
O\in\mathscr{O}_{k}
an orbit, define the
S_{5}
-invariant
orbit contribution

(408)

L_{O}:=\sum_{I\in O}\ell_{I}.

We then define the degree-
k

orbit sum
as the weighted sum of these contributions,

{\mathcal{T}}_{k}:=\sum_{O\in\mathscr{O}_{k}}w_{\bar{O}}L_{O},

and express (
) as the expansion in these orbit sums

\displaystyle 2^{10}{\bm{g}_{\star}}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}\beta^{10-k}{\mathcal{T}}_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\ell_{\mathrm{P}}\,\,+\,\,\cdots\,\,+\,\,42\beta^{10}\ell_{\emptyset}

where
42=w_{{\mathrm{P}}}
. The ellipsis represents a complicated collection of terms.

We note that the conjugation involution (
386
) acts as
C:\ell_{b}\to-\ell_{b}
, and so
C:{\mathcal{T}}_{k}\to(-1)^{k}{\mathcal{T}}_{k}
. Thus, theorem (
3.8
) is equivalent to the following.

Theorem 3.22
.

For
k
odd, the orbit sum
{\mathcal{T}}_{k}
lies in the kernel of the pullback to the hook space. That is

(409)

{\mathcal{T}}_{k}\in\ker\left(\iota:{\mathrm{Sym}}({V_{\mathrm{P}}})\to{\mathrm{Sym}}(V^{(1)}_{\{3,2\}})\right),\quad\text{ for }k\text{ odd }.

In the following subsections, we prove (
3.22
) this statement in each degree individually ((
3.25
), (
3.26
), (
3.27
), (
3.28
)), by showing formulas of the form (for each odd
k
)

{\mathcal{T}}_{k}:=\sum_{O\in\mathscr{O}_{k}}w_{\bar{O}}L_{O}=\sum_{i}Q_{i}

where
w_{\bar{O}}:=w_{{\mathrm{P}}/I}
, for any representative subset
I\in O
, and each
Q_{i}\in\ker(\iota)
is a kernel element given by the following construction.
For
V\in\mathscr{O}_{k}
, let
F
be a function on
{\mathrm{P}}
with support on
\bar{V}
that is invariant under the
V
-stabilizer
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})^{V}
. Then the following degree
k+1
polynomial the
\ell
variables is
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})
invariant

(410)

Q(V,F):=\sum_{I\in V}\ell_{V}\sum_{b\in\bar{V}}F_{b}\ell_{b}=\sum_{O\in\mathscr{O}_{k+1}:V\subset O}F_{O/V}\,[O\!:\!V]\,L_{O}

where
[O\!:\!V]
counts the number of inclusions
V\hookrightarrow O
. This is easily expressed in terms of the orbit sums. Note, if such a function
F\in\mathrm{image}(1\text{-}A)
, then

\sum_{b\in\bar{V}}F_{b}\ell_{b}\in\ker(\iota),

We denote the space of these functions

as

.

Corollary 3.23
.

For

\iota

We now repeat this process of finding such linear combinations of orbit sums that lie in the kernel one degree at a time.

) by a factor of
\tfrac{1}{2}
, for cleaner formulas.

Proposition 3.25
.

The degree 1 orbit sum,

(414)

{\mathcal{T}}_{1}:=\sum_{O\in\mathscr{O}_{1}}w_{\bar{O}}L_{O}=16\,\bullet,

lies in the kernel.

Proof.

Here we only have one orbit
O\in\mathscr{O}_{1}
corresponding to
\bullet
, for which

(415)

w_{\bar{\bullet}}=2(15-3)-9+1=16

There is only one orbit of size
k-1=0
, namely
\emptyset
. There is only a single function on
\bar{\emptyset}=\Gamma
that is invariant under
G^{\emptyset}=G
, that is, the constant function
f_{\Gamma}
.

(416)

-2\,\bullet=-2\sum_{b}\ell_{b}=(1\text{-}A)f_{\Gamma}.

Thus we have shown that

\sum_{O\in\mathscr{O}_{1}}w_{\bar{O}}L_{O}=-8\times Q(\emptyset,\,f_{\Gamma}).

∎

3.4.5.
Degree 9

Lemma 3.29
.

The degree 9 orbit sum
{\mathcal{T}}_{9}
vanishes identically.

Proof.

The only weight is
w(\bullet)=2(0)-1+1=0
, so there is no contribution at this degree.
∎

3.4.6.

We note that the above cancellation does not happen in the even degrees.

We see the kernel contains

v_{4}=3(\bullet)^{2}-5Q(\bullet,f_{\Gamma}+f_{1})

v_{9}=(\bullet)^{2}=4Q(\emptyset,\,f_{\Gamma})^{2}

Thus, we have

{\mathcal{T}}_{2}=5Q(\bullet,f_{\Gamma}+f_{1})+9Q(\emptyset,\,f_{\Gamma})^{2}-\tfrac{3}{4}v_{1}

As the vector
v_{1}
is in the kernel of
A\text{-}1
and thus does not vanish in
{\mathrm{Sym}}^{2}(V_{32})
.

∎

3.5.
Summary

We have thus shown that

(449)

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V^{(1)}_{\{3,2\}}[{\bf{\beta}}])^{S_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}.

4.
hyperplane factorization

We now utilize the extra
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
invariance discussed in the previous section to reveal an unexpected
hyperplane factorization
phenomenon.

4.1.
Boundary data

The hook space has various
boundary hyperplanes
defined by the equations
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}=0
. Relative to these hyperplanes, we need a subtle notion of equivalence for elements of the hook space.

Definition 4.1
.

Consider two Stanley sums
{\bm{s}}_{1},{\bm{s}}_{2}\in\mathsf{SS}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
.

We write

(450)

{\bm{s}}_{1}\simeq{\bm{s}}_{2},

if they become equal when pulled back to the hook space, i.e.
\iota^{*}{\bm{s}}_{1}=\iota^{*}{\bm{s}}_{2}\in\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
.

We write

(451)

{\bm{s}}_{1}\simeq_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}{\bm{s}}_{2},

for a box
b
and hook choice
{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}
, to indicate when

\iota^{*}{\bm{s}}_{1}=\iota^{*}{\bm{s}}_{2}\in\mathsf{R}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}/{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}

That is, they agree in the hook space upon further imposing the relation
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}=0
.

It is easy to check the following result.

Lemma 4.2
.

If
{\bm{s}}_{1}\simeq{\bm{s}}_{2}
and
{\bm{s}}_{1}\simeq_{b}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}{\bm{s}}_{3}
then
{\bm{s}}_{2}\simeq_{b}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}{\bm{s}}_{3}
.
If
{\bm{s}}_{1}\simeq_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}{\bm{s}}_{2}
, then
\bar{\bm{s}}_{1}\simeq_{b}^{\bar{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}\bar{\bm{s}}_{2}
.

Returning back to
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\in(\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321})^{S_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}
. In terms of the above notation, the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
invariance (
3.8
) is expressed as

(452)

{\bm{g}_{\star}}\simeq\bar{\bm{g}_{\star}}.

The following property is perhaps the most surprising of this paper, and is the property that we later claim generalizes for all Jack
Littlewood-Richardson polynomials, see (
6.3
).

Theorem 4.3
.

For each box
b
and hook choice
{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}
, there exists a single diagram
{\bm{E}}(b,{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}})\in\mathsf{SD}_{21,21}^{321}
, so called
boundary datum
, such that

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\simeq_{b}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}{\bm{E}}(b,{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}).

Specifically, for each box
b
we have

(453)

{\bm{E}}(b,{\bm{X}}_{b})={\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}

and

{\bm{E}}(b,\bar{\bm{X}}_{b})=\overline{{\bm{E}}(b,{\bm{X}}_{b})}=\bar{{\bm{X}}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}

This theorem says that when restricted to any boundary hyperplane
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}=0
, the sum of 26 diagrams in
{\bm{g}_{\star}}
collapses to a single diagram,
up to the hook relations
. Note that
none
of the individual boundary datum
{\bm{E}}(b,{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}})
are individually in the support in the sum
{\bm{g}_{\star}}
, i.e. this is purely a hook space phenomena.

Proof.

We first treat the boundary value at
b
corresponding to the hook choice
\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}
, for which we need to show that
{\bm{g}_{\star}}\simeq_{b}^{\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}}{\bm{E}}(b,\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}):=\bar{\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}
. From the formula (
219
), the terms of the Stanley sum agreeing with
{\bm{X}}_{b}
at the box
b
are

{\bm{g}_{\star}}\simeq\bar{\bm{g}_{\star}}\simeq_{b}^{\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}}\sum_{{\bm{D}}:{\bm{D}}_{b}={\bm{X}}_{b}}c_{\bm{D}}\cdot\bar{\bm{D}}=-2\bar{\bm{X}}^{\{b\}}+\sum_{a\sim b}\bar{\bm{X}}^{\{b,a\}}.

We recall the half-kernel sum expression (
402
) of

k_{f}^{0}:=-2\bar{\bm{X}}^{\{b\}}+\sum_{a\sim b}\bar{\bm{X}}^{\{b,a\}}-\bar{\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}.

Thus we have

{\bm{g}_{\star}}\simeq_{b}^{\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}}k_{f}^{0}+\bar{\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}.

Recall the full kernel function (
402
),

{\bm{k}}_{f}=k_{f}^{0}-(k_{f}^{0})^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)},

which vanishes in the hook space by Theorem
3.14
,
{\bm{k}}_{f}\simeq 0
. We can see that
{\bm{k}}_{f}\simeq_{b}^{{\bm{X}}_{b}}k_{f}^{0}
, and so by (
4.2
) we can conclude that
k_{f}^{0}\simeq_{b}^{{\bm{X}}_{b}}0
. Therefore, modulo hook relations, the only surviving boundary contribution is the single diagram
\bar{\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}
, which proves

\bar{\bm{g}_{\star}}\simeq_{b}^{\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}}\bar{\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}=:{\bm{E}}(b,\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}).

For the opposite hook choice, we use the extra conjugation symmetry. Since
{\bm{g}_{\star}}\simeq\bar{\bm{g}_{\star}}
, Lemma
4.2
implies

{\bm{E}}(b,{\bm{X}}_{b})=\overline{{\bm{E}}(b,\bar{\bm{X}}_{b})}={\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}.

∎

The proof of the above theorem demonstrates that one half of the boundary data follows quite easily from the structure of
{\bm{g}_{\star}}
. However, determining the other half required use of the non-manifest
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
symmetry.

Corollary 4.4
.

The boundary data is equivariant under
S_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, i.e.

(454)

g.{\bm{E}}(b,{\bm{X}}_{b})={\bm{E}}(g.b,g.{\bm{X}}_{b}).

Proof.

This follows from
g.{\mathrm{cl}}(b)={\mathrm{cl}}(g.b)
.
∎

.

The Jack Littlewood-Richardson polynomial

5.
Extension to
S_{6}

In this section, we will demonstrate that the
S_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
symmetry group of the Jack Littlewood-Richardson polynomial
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}
has an enhancement to
S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. For this we need to understand the structure of the exotic outer automorphism of
S_{6}
.

5.1.
The outer automorphism of
S_{6}

We draw heavily on the constructions in
[
5
]
.

A
mystic pentagon

P
is a 2-coloring of the edges of
K_{5}
, such that the edges of one color form a 5-cycle (and thus the other colored edges do also). There are six distinct such pentagons, up to exchanging of the two colors.

P
determines a bijection between edges in
K_{5}=K([6]/q)
, where, white edge
A
is sent to black edge
B
when
A
and
B
don’t share any vertices. The remaining vertex is
e
. Such a bijection determines a Pentad
\Sigma_{P}
consisting of the 5 synthemes
\{A/B/\{e,q\}\}
.

Example 5.1
.

The mystic pentagon
(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(4,5),(1,5)
corresponds to the pentad,

\displaystyle\{(1,2)/(3,5)/(4,6)\}

\displaystyle\{(2,3)/(1,4)/(5,6)\}

\displaystyle\{(3,4)/(2,5)/(1,6)\}

\displaystyle\{(4,5)/(1,3)/(2,6)\}

\displaystyle\{(1,5)/(2,4)/(3,6)\}

5.2.
A
\mathbb{Z}_{4}
action on
3
-subsets

For a choice of mystic pentagon
P
we construct a permutation
\rho_{P}\in\mathrm{Perm}\binom{[6]}{3}
on the set of
3
-subsets of six elements. Let
q\in[6]
be the vertex not included in
P
.

For
T\in\binom{[6]}{3}
, either
q\in T
, or
q\in T^{c}
, so denote by
(-1)^{q\notin T}T
the one that contains
q
. From this, define the duad

d_{T}:=((-1)^{q\notin T}T)\setminus\{q\}.

Note
d_{T}=d_{T^{c}}
.
d_{T}
is a member of a unique syntheme
S\in\Sigma_{P}
, of the form

S=\{d_{T}/d^{\prime}/\{e,q\}\}.

We define
D(T):=\{q\}\cup d^{\prime}\in\binom{[6]}{3}
. Then we see that
D(D(T))=\{q\}\cup d_{T}=(-1)^{q\notin T}T
, and the only four 3-subsets that map to
S
are
d^{-1}(S)=\{T,D(T),T^{c},D(T)^{c}\}
. The map
\rho
will cycle these four 3-subsets, the only question is in which direction. For a duad
d
, let
(-1)^{P(d)}=1
if
P|_{d}
is white, and
(-1)
otherwise. We define

\rho_{P}(T):=(-1)^{q\notin T}(-1)^{P({d_{T}})}D(T).

Corollary 5.2
.

\rho^{2}_{P}=c

Thus
\rho_{P}
is order
4
, and splits up the 20 3-subsets into 5 4-cycles of the form
(T,U,T^{c},U^{c})
.

5.2.1.
The Johnson Graphs
J(n,k,i)

For an
n
-element set,
[n]
, consider the set of all
k
-subsets of elements, denoted
\binom{[n]}{k}
, and define the distance between two
k
-subsets as
d(T,T^{\prime}):=k-|T\cap T^{\prime}|
. The set
\binom{[n]}{k}
forms the vertices of the Johnson graph
J(n,k,i)
, with an edge
T\sim T^{\prime}
between two
k
-subsets
T,T^{\prime}
when
|T\cap T^{\prime}|=i
, i.e.
T
and
T^{\prime}
share
i
elements, so
d(T,T^{\prime})=1
. Clearly, this distance agrees with the usual graph theoretic distance.

We will mainly be interested in the Johnson Graph,
{\mathrm{J}}:=J(6,3):=J(6,3,2)
,
which has
\binom{6}{3}=20
vertices, and each vertex has
9
neighbours differing by one element.

Theorem 5.3

(
[
3
, Theorem 9.1.2]
)
.

{\mathrm{Aut}}(J(2k,k))=S_{2k}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}

where
S_{2k}
acts in the standard way on the set of
2k
elements, and
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
is generated by conjugation
C
.

Figure 3
.
The 2-coloring of the vertices of
J(6,3)
that partitions it into two copies of the Petersen graph. The copies are exchanged under complementation.
\rho
permutes the four elements on any line that goes through the origin, and exchanges the inner ring with the outer ring.

Lemma 5.4
.

d(T,U)=2\leftrightarrow d(\rho(T),\rho(U))=1

Thus
\rho
is not an automorphism of the Johnson graph, but rather implements an isomorphism between
J(6,3,2)
and
J(6,3,1)
.

As noted in
[
5
]
section 1.2, there is a bijection between mystic pentagons and 2-colorings of
{\mathrm{J}}
such that each
T
and
T^{c}
have different colors and every
K_{4}
subgraph has two vertices of each color. The next construction agrees with this bijection.

Corollary 5.5
.

For
(ij)
in
\binom{[5]}{2}
, the map

(525)

\gamma:(ij)\mapsto\rho_{P}(ij6)

gives an embedding of the Petersen graph
{\mathrm{P}}
into the Johnson graph
{\mathrm{J}}
. Composing with conjugation gives a complementary embedding
\gamma^{c}
, which provides a partition of the vertices
{\mathrm{J}}=\gamma({\mathrm{P}})\cup{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\gamma^{c}({\mathrm{P}})}}
. As we vary the choice of pentad
P
, we find all 12 embeddings
{\mathrm{P}}\hookrightarrow{\mathrm{J}}
.

The stabiliser of this
\gamma({\mathrm{P}})
is the
S_{5}={\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})
conjugated by
\rho
.

Lemma 5.6
.

The embedding
\sigma_{ij}\mapsto s_{ij}
of
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}})=S_{5}\hookrightarrow{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{J}})=S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
that intertwines
\gamma
takes the form

s_{12}=-(46)(15)(23),

s_{23}=-(56)(12)(34),

s_{34}=-(16)(23)(45),

s_{45}=-(26)(15)(34).

That is,

s_{ij}\gamma=\gamma\sigma_{ij}.

This is the embedding
(\tau,{\mathrm{sgn}})
, where
\tau
is the exotic inclusion of
S_{5}\hookrightarrow S_{6}
determined by the pentad
P
.

5.3.
Vertex Representations

Let
\tilde{V_{\mathrm{J}}}
be the vertex representation of
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{J}})=S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, i.e. the vector space with a generator
y_{T}
for each
3
-subset
T
.
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{J}})
acts on
\tilde{V_{\mathrm{J}}}
by
g.y_{T}=y_{g.T}
. The adjacency matrix
A_{\mathrm{J}}
commutes with
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{J}})
, under which we find

Lemma 5.7
.

Under
{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{J}})\times{\mathbb{C}}[A_{\mathrm{J}}]
, we have

(526)

\tilde{V_{\mathrm{J}}}\cong V_{6,{\mathrm{id}}}^{(9)}\oplus V_{42,{\mathrm{id}}}^{(-1)}\oplus V_{33,{\mathrm{sgn}}}^{(-3)}\oplus V_{51,{\mathrm{sgn}}}^{(3)},

with dimensions

(20)=(1)+(9)+(5)+(5).

Proof.

The spectrum and multiplicities are given in
[
3
, Theorems 9.1.2, 8.4.2-3]
. We describe each of these two
5
-dimensional sub-representations.
The map
\iota:V_{51}\to{V_{\mathrm{J}}}
is given by
\{x_{i}\}\mapsto y_{T}=x_{T}:=\sum_{t\in T}x_{t}
, which satisfies
x_{T}+x_{T^{c}}=0
.

The sub-representation
V_{33}\subset{V_{\mathrm{J}}}
is spanned by the elements

(527)

\gamma(cl_{b}):=y_{\gamma(b)}-\sum_{a\sim b}y_{\gamma(a)}

where
\gamma
is the embedding (
525
) of the Petersen graph into the Johnson graph.
These are clearly invariant under
\gamma({\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathrm{P}}))
.

∎

We will consider the 10-dimensional anti-symmetric vertex representation,
{V_{\mathrm{J}}}:=(\tilde{V_{\mathrm{J}}})_{{\mathrm{sgn}}}
, that is, we impose
y_{T}=-y_{T^{c}}
. Following from (
526
), this is given as

{V_{\mathrm{J}}}\cong V_{33,{\mathrm{sgn}}}^{(-3)}\oplus V_{51,{\mathrm{sgn}}}^{(3)}.

acting on

Proof.

For this, we look at the claw relation
cl_{b}:=\ell_{b}-\sum_{a\sim b}\ell_{a}=0
of any vertex
b

\sigma
maps it to the linear span of such claws, hence the subspace
V_{32}
is invariant. Up to
S_{4}
invariance, there are only two such claws. Either
b
is fixed or
b
is swapped by
\sigma
. Take the fixed vertex
(15)
in the graph
535
. We find
\sigma(cl_{(15)})=(15)+(14)+(13)+(12)=(15)-cl_{(25)}+(25)-(34)+(12)=-cl_{(25)}-cl_{(34)}
. For the non-fixed vertex
24
, we find
\sigma(cl_{(24)})=cl_{(24)}
, which finishes the proof.

5.4.
Extra invariance

Proposition 5.11
.

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V_{32}[{\bf{\beta}}])^{S_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}
is invariant under
\sigma_{56}\in\mathrm{End}(V_{32})
.

Proof.

Under the branching
S_{5}
to this
S_{4}
, we have
V_{32}\to V_{22}\oplus V_{31}
, a
2\oplus 3
split, on which
\sigma_{56}
must act as block diagonal
\sigma_{56}=(-1)^{a}\oplus(-1)^{b}
. Since
V_{32}\cong V_{33}
as an
S_{6}
representation,
\mathrm{Tr}_{V_{33}}(\sigma_{56})=1=2(-1)^{a}+3(-1)^{b}
. Thus
\sigma_{56}
acts as
(-1)\oplus(1)
.

Since
S_{4}
acts as reflections on
V_{22}
,
{\mathbb{C}}[V_{22}]^{S_{4}}\cong{\mathbb{C}}[f_{2},f_{3}]
is a polynomial ring. By standard theory,
{\mathbb{C}}[V_{31}]^{S_{4}}\cong{\mathbb{C}}[e_{2},e_{3}]
, So

{\mathbb{C}}[V_{32}]^{S_{4}}={\mathbb{C}}[f_{2},f_{3}^{\mathrm{sgn}},e_{2},e_{3}]

On which
\sigma_{56}
acts as
-1
on
f_{3}
, and the other generators are invariant. Thus, the only polynomials of degree 10 or less that are anti-invariant are

f_{3}e_{3}\{1,e_{2},f_{2},e_{2}^{2},e_{2}f_{2},f_{2}^{2}\}

Thus, any anti-invariant must have at degree
6,8
or
10
. We prove that
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}
has no anti-invariant component in each of these degrees.
First, in degree 10,
({{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}})_{(10)}=2\prod_{b}\ell_{b}
, which under
\sigma_{56}
produces a factor of
(-1)^{6}
, and hence is invariant.

In degree 8, we split up the two
S_{5}
orbits into
S_{4}
orbits, then compute the action of
\sigma_{56}
on those orbits.

S_{5}
orbit

S_{4}
orbits

We require
E_{0}
to vanish, which can only happen via one of two ways: either the sum of weights
(W_{0})
vanishes, or the
S_{4}
-orbit sum
(\mathcal{O}_{0})
vanishes under the pullback to
V_{32}
. In degree 8, there are no kernel functions on
{\mathrm{P}}
of the form
(1\text{-}A_{\mathrm{P}})f
that are supported on only two vertices. Thus, we cannot show that the orbit sums
\mathcal{O}_{0}
vanish when pulled back to
V_{32}
. So, we are required to force the weight sum
W_{0}
to vanish. This is

where, as before,
\mathcal{O}_{i}
is the anti-invariant orbit pair in
e_{I}
. Hence,

Q_{1}=2\mathcal{O}_{2}+2\mathcal{O}_{3}+\mathcal{O}_{4},\quad Q_{2}=3\mathcal{O}_{4}.

Both of these combinations vanish in the pullback to
V_{32}
, i.e.

\iota^{*}\mathcal{O}_{4}=0=\iota^{*}(\mathcal{O}_{2}+\mathcal{O}_{3})\,\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{6}(V_{32}).

Now, we have
W_{2}=W_{3}
so our combination
E_{2}+E_{3}=\tfrac{1}{2}w_{2}(\mathcal{O}_{2}+\mathcal{O}_{3})
vanishes, and so does
E_{4}\sim\mathcal{O}_{4}
. Thus the last three orbit sums contributions vanish,
E_{2}+E_{3}+E_{4}=0
.

However, our orbit sum
\mathcal{O}_{1}
does not vanish when restricted to
V_{32}
, so it is genuinely anti-invariant (i.e. proportional to
f_{3}e_{3}
), which means that the weight sum
w_{1}
must vanish. So we find just a single equation in degree 6 that must be satisfied in order for
({{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}})_{(6)}
to be invariant under
\sigma_{56}
, and that is

W_{1}:=w(\hbox to17.79pt{\vbox to10.59pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 8.8971pt\lower-5.29706pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -7.61 4.98 C -7.61 6.28 -8.67 7.33 -9.96 7.33 C -11.26 7.33 -12.31 6.28 -12.31 4.98 C -12.31 3.68 -11.26 2.63 -9.96 2.63 C -8.67 2.63 -7.61 3.68 -7.61 4.98 Z M -9.96 4.98}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

5.4.1.
Boundary Hyperplanes Again

Let
T
denote the 3-subsets of
[6]
, which carries the action of
S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. Consider the 20 hyperplanes
H_{T}:=x_{T}-\beta=0
, which we easily see are permuted by
S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. The polytope defined by these 20 hyperplanes contains the 12 points in the orbit of

\tfrac{\beta}{3}\{5,-1,-1,-1,-1,-1\}\in V_{51}

Each such point lies on
10
of the hyperplanes (the 10 choices of 3
T
that include
+5
, or the 10 choices that include three
+1
’s), and each hyperplane contains 6 such points.

Lemma 5.12
.

The polynomial
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}
has the following properties.

•

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V_{51}[{\bf{\beta}}])^{S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}

•

For each triple
T
, consider the degree 10 polynomial
J_{T}:=\prod_{S:S\cap T\leq 1}H_{S}
. Each
J_{T}
is invariant under
x_{S}\to x_{S^{c}}
,
\beta\to-\beta
. Then, on each hyperplane
H_{T}=0
, we have a factorization

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}|_{H_{T}=0}=J_{T}|_{H_{T}=0}.

Proof.

By Theorem
4.3
, on each hook hyperplane
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}=0
we have
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\simeq{\bm{E}}(b,{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}})
, a product of
10
hooks. Under the embedding
\gamma
, the hook
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{{\bm{X}}_{b}}
corresponds to
H_{\gamma(b)}
and
{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\bar{\bm{X}}_{b}}
to
H_{\gamma^{c}(b)}
. The boundary datum
{\bm{X}}^{{\mathrm{cl}}(b)}
is the diagram with hooks flipped on
{\mathrm{cl}}(b)
, so its
10
factors are
H_{\gamma(a)}
for
a\notin{\mathrm{cl}}(b)
and
H_{\gamma^{c}(a)}
for
a\in{\mathrm{cl}}(b)
. Setting
T:=\gamma(b)
,

For
a\notin{\mathrm{cl}}(b)
: since
\gamma
is a graph embedding, Petersen non-adjacency gives
|\gamma(a)\cap\gamma(b)|\neq 2
, and
a\neq b
gives
\gamma(a)\neq\gamma(b)
, so
|\gamma(a)\cap T|\leq 1
.

For
a\in{\mathrm{cl}}(b)
:
|\gamma^{c}(a)\cap T|=|\gamma(a)^{c}\cap\gamma(b)|=3-|\gamma(a)\cap\gamma(b)|\leq 1
, since
a=b
or
a\sim b
gives
|\gamma(a)\cap\gamma(b)|\geq 2
.

∎

5.4.2.
Invariant Rings

As the
S_{5}
representation
V_{32}
is not generated by reflections, the invariant ring
{\mathbb{C}}[V_{32}]^{S_{5}}
is not a free polynomial ring
2
2

2

From computations in Sage, it appears to be the case that

C[V_{32}]^{S_{5}}=
(C[e_{2},e_{3},e_{4},e_{5},e_{6}]\otimes C[r_{6},r_{7},r_{8},r_{9},r_{15}])/(r_{i}\cdot r_{j}=a_{ij}^{0}(e)+a_{ij}^{k}(e)r_{k})
, where the
e_{i}
are the elementary polynomials pulled back from
V_{51}
.

.
Thus any expression for
{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}^{10}(V_{32}[{\bf{\beta}}])^{S_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}
in terms of
{\mathbb{C}}[V_{32}]^{S_{5}}
would likely contain redundancies. However, now we have ‘untwisted’ from
V_{32}
to
V_{51}
, whose invariant ring is generated by elementary symmetric polynomials

{\mathbb{C}}[V_{51}]^{S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}={\mathbb{C}}[e_{2},e_{3},e_{4},e_{5},e_{6}]^{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}.

Observation 5.13
.

In the invariant ring
{\mathbb{C}}[V_{51}]^{S_{6}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}}
, we find

\displaystyle{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}

\displaystyle=42\beta^{10}+54e_{2}\beta^{8}+(34e_{4}+14e_{2}^{2})\beta^{6}

(578)

\displaystyle\quad+(42e_{6}+30e_{3}^{2}+4e_{2}e_{4}+2e_{2}^{3})\beta^{4}

\displaystyle\quad+(-8e_{4}^{2}-18e_{3}e_{5}+12e_{2}e_{6}+6e_{2}e_{3}^{2}+2e_{2}^{2}e_{4})\beta^{2}

\displaystyle\quad+(2e_{5}^{2}-8e_{4}e_{6}+2e_{3}^{2}e_{4}-2e_{2}e_{3}e_{5}+2e_{2}^{2}e_{6}).

We can also look at the expansion in monomial symmetric functions

{{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}=\sum_{\lambda:|\lambda|\leq 10}a_{\lambda}m_{\lambda}\beta^{10-|\lambda|}.

Lemma 5.14
.

The monomial coefficient
a_{\lambda}
can be non-zero only if
\lambda_{1}\leq 3
.

Proof.

We use the expression of
F
in terms of the Johnson graph variables
y_{T}:=x_{T_{1}}+x_{T_{2}}+x_{T_{3}}
on the anti-symmetric quotient
{V_{\mathrm{J}}}
(where
y_{T}=-y_{T^{c}}
). Under the embedding
\psi:{V_{\mathrm{P}}}\to{V_{\mathrm{J}}}
, the polynomial
F
is written as a degree-10 polynomial in these
y_{T}
variables. Each
y_{T}
is a
linear
combination of the
x_{i}
with coefficients
0
or
\pm 1
, and each
y_{T}
involves exactly
3
of the
6
variables
x_{i}
.

The exponent of
x_{i}
in a monomial
\prod_{j=1}^{k}y_{T_{j}}
equals the number of
T_{j}
containing
i
. Among the
10
anti-symmetric representatives, element
i
appears in exactly
\binom{5}{2}=10
triples, but by
S_{6}
symmetry the maximum exponent of any
x_{i}
in the support of
F
is constrained. The key observation is that in the
\ell
-variable formula, each factor
(\ell_{b}\pm\beta)
contributes, via the map
\psi
, a linear form in at most
3
of the
x_{i}
’s. Since
F
is
S_{6}
-invariant and degree
10
, expanding in monomial symmetric functions

on

, the leading part
\lambda_{1}
cannot exceed
3
because each linear factor
y_{T}
distributes its contribution equally among
3
variables.
∎

That is,
\psi
maps between these two Stanley diagrams,

\psi:{\bm{g}}_{21,21}^{2211}\to{\bm{E}}(c_{4},{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}).

Although, this map
does not
preserve the relations between these hooks.
But, rather, there exists a modification
\tilde{\psi}
of
\psi
given by,

\displaystyle{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(a)\mapsto

\displaystyle{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(a)

\displaystyle{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(c)\mapsto

\displaystyle-{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(c)

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{+{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(b)}}

\displaystyle\tilde{\psi}:\qquad{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(d)\mapsto

\displaystyle-{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(d)

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{+{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(b)}}

\displaystyle{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(e)\mapsto

\displaystyle{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(e)

\displaystyle\ {\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(f)\mapsto

\displaystyle-{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(f)

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{+{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(b)}}

\displaystyle{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(b)\mapsto

\displaystyle-{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(b)

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{+{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(b)}}.

such that

[\tilde{\psi}({\bm{h}}_{a})]=[{\bm{h}}_{a}],\,\,\forall a\neq b

[\tilde{\psi}({\bm{h}}_{b})]=0

Crucially, this map is only of the form (
612
) modulo
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{1}}(b)}}
.

For example
\tilde{\psi}
induces an equality of
hook lengths
modulo
3+2\alpha=h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(b)
. e.g. for box
d
,

\tilde{\psi}:2+2\alpha\mapsto-(1+0\alpha)\mod 3+2\alpha.

We now formalize this construction.

Definition 6.1
.

A
hook correspondence
between two adjacent triples
T_{2}\to T_{1}
(via a pivot at
b\in\sigma_{1}\cap\sigma_{2}
) is a linear map
\tilde{\psi}
between hook variables such that

•

\tilde{\psi}
has the form
{\bm{h}}_{T_{2}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}(a)\mapsto\pm{\bm{h}}_{T_{1}}^{\pm{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}(a^{\prime})
modulo
{\bm{h}}_{\sigma_{2}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(b)
.

•

\tilde{\psi}:{\bm{h}}_{\sigma_{2}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}(b)\mapsto 0
.

•

\tilde{\psi}
preserves the image of the evaluation map,

[\tilde{\psi}({\bm{h}}_{a})]=[{\bm{h}}_{a}],\,\,\forall a\neq b

In other words, when working on the hyperplane
{\bm{h}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda_{2}}(b)=0
, we find a bijection of the hooks (with flips) that preserves evaluation.

6.1.1.
General correspondences

The above example is of a simple form, which we describe as an action on Stanley diagrams. Given partition
\lambda
, pick two outer corners
a,b\in\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}
, let
d=a\vee b
. The two partitions
\lambda+a
,
\lambda+b
thus differ by a single box move. We will describe a hook correspondence
\psi_{d}
on Stanley diagrams from
\lambda+a
to
\lambda+b
, which acts as identity on the other two partitions (
\mu,\nu
), and as identity on the row-column set of
a
and
b
.

Note
h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}_{\lambda+a}(d)=h^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}_{\lambda+b}(d)
. The rule for
\psi_{d}
is as follows. If a box is to the left of
d
, its hook assignment is swapped with the box on the corresponding other row. Similarly for those boxes beneath
d
, they are exchanged with the box in the other column. For the remaining highlighted boxes something more subtle occurs. If
b
is in a row with a outer corner (i.e. a place where a box can be added to
\lambda
), then the hook is sent to the box beneath that outer corner, and it is flipped (lower
\leftrightarrow
upper). If
b
is not in a row with an outer corner, then it moves down one. Next, if a box is to the right of
b
, then if it is a column with an inner corner (i.e. where a box can be removed) then it is swapped with the box to the left of that outer corner (and flipped). If there is no such inner corner, it is moved to the right. All other boxes (i.e. non-highlighted) remain unchanged.

The above map is always a hook correspondence, as is demonstrated by the following lemma.

Lemma 6.2
.

For
a,b\in\mathcal{O}_{\mu}
, with
a<b
. Let
x:=h_{\mu+a}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}(a\vee b)=h_{\mu+b}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}(a\vee b)
.
For
c\in\mathcal{O}_{\mu}
, we have,
if
a<c<b

h_{\mu+b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(b\vee c)+h_{\mu+a}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}(a\vee c)=x

if
c<a

h_{\mu+b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(b\vee c)-h_{\mu+a}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}(a\vee c)=x

if
b<c

-h_{\mu+b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(b\vee c)+h_{\mu+a}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}(a\vee c)=x

For
c\in\mathcal{I}_{\mu}
, we have, if
a<c<b

h_{\mu+b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(a\vee c)+h_{\mu+a}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(b\vee c)=x

if
c<a

h_{\mu+b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(a\vee c)-h_{\mu+a}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}(b\vee c)=x

if
b<c

-h_{\mu+b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(a\vee c)+h_{\mu+a}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(b\vee c)=x

6.1
), there are four such hook correspondences of this form (up to basic symmetries) for

6.1.2.
Extension to window families

Let
b=(0,0)
, and
{\mathcal{W}}^{\prime}
be the window family for
\{21,21,2211\}
defined by (
2.5
). For each
W^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{W}}^{\prime}
, we claim there exists a window
W\in{\mathcal{W}}
of
\{21,21,321\}
and a hook correspondence
\tilde{\psi}_{W^{\prime},W}:W^{\prime}\to W
relative to
b
.
This data defines a map

(719)

\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{2211}({\mathcal{W}}^{\prime})/\{{\bm{h}}_{c_{4}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}\}\to\mathsf{R}_{21,21}^{321}({\mathcal{W}})/\{{\bm{h}}_{c_{4}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}\}

Thus, in summary, we interpret the simplification (
6.1
) in terms of the hook correspondences
\tilde{\psi}
inducing a local equivalence between Jack LR coefficients,

(720)

\tilde{\psi}:{\bm{g}}_{21,21;2211}\mod{\bm{h}}_{2211}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}}(b)\,\,\,\mapsto\,\,\,{\bm{g}}_{21,21;321}\mod{\bm{h}}_{321}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}(b).

We conjecture this property holds in general.

Conjecture 6.3

(To appear in
[
8
]
)
.

Let
(\mu_{1}\nu_{1}\lambda_{1})
and
(\mu_{2}\nu_{2}\lambda_{2})
be
adjacent
triples of partitions corresponding to a pivot at
b
. There exists a family of hook correspondences
\tilde{\psi}
between window families
{\mathcal{W}}^{\prime},{\mathcal{W}}
which induce a map

(721)

\{\tilde{\psi}\}:\mathsf{R}_{\mu_{1}\nu_{1}}^{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{W}}^{\prime})/\{{\bm{h}}_{b}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}\}\to\mathsf{R}_{\mu_{2}\nu_{2}}^{\lambda_{2}}({\mathcal{W}})/\{{\bm{h}}_{b^{\prime}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}\}

under which we have the equivalence

(722)

\tilde{\psi}:{\bm{g}}_{\mu_{1}\nu_{1};\lambda_{1}}\mod{\bm{h}}_{\sigma_{1}}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}(b)\,\,\,\mapsto\,\,\,{\bm{g}}_{\mu_{2}\nu_{2};\lambda_{2}}\mod{\bm{h}}_{\sigma_{2}}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{A}}}}(b)

6.2.
Consequences for LR coefficients

Conjecture (
6.3
) has a concrete manifestation at the level of regular LR coefficients
4
4

4

P. Alexandersson has calculated many of these coefficients in
[
1
]

of the adjacent pair of triples of the previous example. These are given by

(723)

\displaystyle g_{21,21;321}(\alpha)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 6\alpha^{4}(1+2\alpha)(2+\alpha)(2+11\alpha+2\alpha^{2}),

(724)

\displaystyle g_{21,21;2211}(\alpha)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 4\alpha^{4}(1+2\alpha)^{2}(3+\alpha)(4+\alpha).

Now, the relation of Jack LR polynomials of (
720
) becomes a more direct equivalence of Jack LR functions,

(725)

g_{21,21;2211}(\alpha)\equiv\,g_{21,21;321}(\alpha)\mod h_{321}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}(c_{4}).

In other words the
difference
of these polynomials

g_{21,21;321}(\alpha)-g_{21,21;2211}(\alpha)=2\alpha^{4}(1+2\alpha){\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(3+2\alpha)}(-4+6\alpha+\alpha^{2})

is divisible by
h_{321}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}(c_{4})={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(3+2\alpha)}
.
Indeed, we have

g_{21,21;321}(-3/2)=g_{21,21;2211}(-3/2)=\tfrac{1215}{4}.

We conjecture that this divisibility holds in general. Conjecture
6.3
immediately implies the following statement, which is more directly verifiable.

Conjecture 6.4
.

For two triples of partitions
(\mu_{1},\nu_{1},\lambda_{1})
,
(\mu_{2},\nu_{2},\lambda_{2})
that differ by a single box move (a ‘pivot’) in one of the pairs in the triples, say at
b_{1}\in\sigma_{1}
,
b_{2}\in\sigma_{2}
, so that

h_{\sigma_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}({b_{1}})=h_{\sigma_{2}}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}({b_{2}}),

then we have

(726)

g_{\mu_{1}\nu_{1};\lambda_{1}}(\alpha)\equiv\,g_{\mu_{2}\nu_{2};\lambda_{2}}(\alpha)\mod h_{\sigma_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}({b_{1}}).

This above conjecture is the strongest evidence we have for the approach to understanding Jack LR coefficients developed in this work.

Example 6.5
.

We consider two pivots for the
c=3
Jack LR

\displaystyle g_{{321},{221};{43211}}=48\alpha^{5}(2+\alpha)(1+2\alpha)^{2}\times

\displaystyle(120+1220\alpha+5574\alpha^{2}+12443\alpha^{3}+13849\alpha^{4}+7655\alpha^{5}+2073\alpha^{6}+254\alpha^{7}+12\alpha^{8})

.

First at the box
b=(0,0)
in
\lambda_{1}=43211
, for which
h_{\lambda_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}={\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(5+3\alpha)}
. This pivots to the
c=1
coefficient

g_{{321},{221};{332111}}=96\alpha^{5}(1+\alpha)(3+\alpha)^{2}(4+\alpha)(1+2\alpha)^{4}(5+2\alpha)(2+3\alpha).

The difference is

48\alpha^{5}(1+2\alpha)^{2}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(5+3\alpha)}(-96-556\alpha-750\alpha^{2}+676\alpha^{3}+2155\alpha^{4}+1596\alpha^{5}+501\alpha^{6}+70\alpha^{7}+4\alpha^{8}).

Secondly we pivot at the box
b=(0,0)
in
\mu
, for which
h_{\mu}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}(b)={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(3+2\alpha)}
, which pivots to the coefficient

\displaystyle g_{{2211},{221};{43211}}=128\alpha^{5}(1+\alpha)(3+\alpha)(4+\alpha)(1+2\alpha)(2+3\alpha)\times

\displaystyle(12+131\alpha+321\alpha^{2}+294\alpha^{3}+97\alpha^{4}+9\alpha^{5}).

The difference
g_{{321},{221};{43211}}-g_{{2211},{221};{43211}}
is

\displaystyle-16\alpha^{5}(1+2\alpha){\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(3+2\alpha)}\times

\displaystyle(-528-7360\alpha-26336\alpha^{2}-35740\alpha^{3}-11003\alpha^{4}+16523\alpha^{5}+15493\alpha^{6}+5025\alpha^{7}+690\alpha^{8}+36\alpha^{9}).

The equations (
726
) give a large family of compatibility relations between all Jack LR coefficients. However, these alone are not sufficient to completely determine them all, although it is the case that this conjecture strongly constrains the Strong form of the Stanley conjecture (
1.3
). Only at the level of Jack LR
polynomials
are these local compatibilities sufficient to determine the polynomials entirely.

6.3.
Extension to Shifted Jacks

In

]

J^{\#}_{\lambda}(\alpha)
, which are non-homogenous extensions of the Jack functions
J_{\lambda}(\alpha)
. The products of shifted Jacks are captured by the shifted Jack LR coefficients
5
5

5

The notation of
[
2
]
is
\tilde{d}_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}
for our
g_{\mu\nu;\lambda}
.

g_{\mu\nu;\lambda}
, where now
|\lambda|\leq|\mu|+|\nu|
.

Conjecture 6.6
.

Conjecture (
6.4
) holds for shifted Jack Littlewood-Richardson coefficients.

We have no conceptual explanation for this observation, other than its connection to regular Jack LR coefficients. We have not been able to determine if any windowing properties hold in the shifted case.

6.4.
Extension to Macdonald Polynomials

Consider
P_{\mu}(q,t)
the integral Macdonald functions. We define the Macdonald Littlewood-Richardson coefficients
g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}(q,t)
, by

J_{\mu}(q,t)\cdot J_{\nu}(q,t)=\sum_{\lambda}g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}(q,t)J_{\lambda}(q,t).

As before, we set

g_{\mu\nu;\lambda}(q,t):=g_{\mu\nu}^{\lambda}(q,t)\langle J_{\lambda}\rangle^{2}_{q,t}.

The
modified
Macdonald LR coefficients are

(729)

\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu;\lambda}(q,t):=t^{n(\mu)+n(\nu)-n(\lambda)}g_{\mu\nu;\lambda}(q,t^{-1})

We suspect that the structure of Macdonald Littlewood-Richardson coefficients should exhibit all of the same properties as those for Jacks.

Conjecture 6.9
.

Let
(\mu_{1},\nu_{1},\lambda_{1})
,
(\mu_{2},\nu_{2},\lambda_{2})
be two triples of partitions that differ by a single box move (a ‘pivot’) in one of the pairs in the triples, say at
b_{1}\in\sigma_{1}
,
b_{2}\in\sigma_{2}
, so that the
(q,t)
-hook lengths
6

6

.
agree

h_{\sigma_{1}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{U}}}({b_{1}})=h_{\sigma_{2}}^{{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{L}}}}({b_{2}})=1-q^{y}t^{x}.

Let
\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu;\lambda}(q,t)
be the modified Macdonald Littlewood-Richardson coefficient (
729
).
If
x\neq y
, then we have a simple ratio of evaluations at the zero of the common hook

,

\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}{q\to s^{x}}\\
{t\to s^{-y}}\end{subarray}}\left(\frac{\,\,\tilde{g}_{\mu_{1}\nu_{1};\lambda_{1}}(q,t^{-1})}{\tilde{g}_{\mu_{2}\nu_{2};\lambda_{2}}(q,t^{-1})}\right)\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}.

Note: only with the normalization of
t^{n(\mu)+\ldots}
coming from (

) that the right hand side is a constant, a requirement not present in the Jack case (

then there can be a mismatch of the order of vanishing, but we expect that this case can be included with correct normalizations. We also expect that with normalizations the RHS can made to be

7.
Appendix

7.1.
Root systems

Speculatively, we rephrase the hyperplane factorization properties in terms of the root system
A_{5}
. Let
\mathfrak{h}=V_{5,1}
, the root vectors are
\alpha_{ij}=e_{i}-e_{j}\in\mathfrak{h}
.

The automorphism group of the Root system
A_{5}
is given by the Weyl group
W(A_{5})=S_{6}
adjoined the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
automorphism of the Dynkin diagram (
-w_{0}
). Thus

The
\binom{6}{3}
weights of
\wedge^{3}
are given by
\mu_{T}:=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i\in T}e_{i}-\sum_{i\in T^{c}}e_{i}\right)
. We have

\mu_{abi}-\mu_{abj}=\alpha_{ij},

reflecting that
\wedge^{3}
is a minuscule representation.

Corollary 7.1
.

The weight graph of the representation
\wedge^{3}
is
J(6,3)
.

The local factorization property for
F={{{{\bm{G}}}}_{\star}}
takes the form

F\big|_{\langle\mu,x\rangle=\beta}=W_{\mu}\big|_{\langle\mu,x\rangle=\beta}

where

W_{\mu}(x,\beta):=\prod_{\nu\in\bar{N}(\mu)}\bigl(\langle\nu,x\rangle+\beta\bigr)

Lemma 7.2
.

1)

If
d(T,U)=1
, then the two local factorisations agree on the intersection of the weight hyperplanes.

2)

If
d(T,U)>1
, then the two local factorisations vanish on the intersection of the weight hyperplanes.

Proof.

For part
(1)
if
\mu_{T}\sim\mu_{U}
, then there exists a root
\alpha
such that
\mu_{T}-\mu_{U}=\alpha
, ie
s_{\alpha}(\mu_{T})=\mu_{U}
. For
x
in the intersection of hyperplanes
\mu_{T}(x)=-\beta=\mu_{U}(x)
, we find
\alpha(x)=0
and so
s_{\alpha}(x)=x
. Thus

\prod_{\mu^{\prime}\in\bar{N}(\mu)}\bigl(\langle\mu^{\prime},x\rangle+\beta\bigr)

\bar{N}(s_{\alpha}(\mu))=s_{\alpha}\bar{N}(\mu)

For part (2), we use the fact that for
J(6,3)
we have
d(T,U)>1\leftrightarrow U\in\bar{N}(\mu_{T})
.
∎

Observation 7.3
.

For
\rho=(-5,-3,-1,1,3,5)
which is twice the Weyl vector of
A_{5}
, we have

F(t\rho,\beta)=42\prod_{i=1}^{6}(\beta+t\rho_{i})^{q_{i}}

where
q=(1,2,2,2,2,1)
.

The image of the positive lattice in Dynkin coordinates, i.e.
\langle\alpha_{i},x(w)\rangle
for
x(w)
given by (
580
), is

\alpha_{0}=-4(1+\alpha)-2(w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{4}+w_{5})

\alpha_{1}=2(1+\alpha)+2(w_{1}+w_{5})

\alpha_{2}=2(1+\alpha)+2(w_{3}+w_{4})

\alpha_{3}=2(1+\alpha)+2(w_{2}+w_{5})

\alpha_{4}=-4(1+\alpha)-2(w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3}+w_{5})

It is an interesting question whether similar functions exist for other root systems with a choice of minuscule representation.

Example 7.4
.

For the
A_{3}
root system, the function

f_{\omega_{2}}:=6\beta^{5}+8e_{2}\beta^{3}+(2e_{2}^{2}-8e_{4})\beta,

is
W(A_{3})=S_{4}
invariant, anti-invariant under
(x,\beta)\to(-w_{0}x,-\beta)
, and satisfies the hyperplane factorization formula for the weight graph of
V_{\omega_{2}}=\wedge^{2}({\mathbb{C}}^{4})
,

Calculations show that a (somewhat trivial) solution exists for
\{A_{n},\omega_{\mathrm{std}}\}
for all
n
, and non-trivially for
\{B_{n},\omega_{\mathrm{spin}}\}
for
n=3,4,5
.
